podcasts.title: The Inside Story of the 50 Who Built Modern AI With Kevin Roose
podcasts.transcript:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:17
A couple years ago, you know, we had to fact check the AIs, and now the AIs fact check me. I'm playing with everything. Literally, like, I can't keep track. I have agents now that are, like, correcting my other agents. It's a huge mess.

Speaker 2 | 00:18 - 00:19
The AGI Chronicles.

Speaker 3 | 00:19 - 00:21
It was so good.

Speaker 2 | 00:21 - 00:21
Was it?

Speaker 3 | 00:21 - 00:22
It was phenomenal.

Speaker 2 | 00:22 - 00:23
Why did you like it?

Speaker 3 | 00:24 - 00:31
Like, it addresses the question that so many of us have when it comes to this moment in AI, which is just like, how did we get here?

Speaker 2 | 00:31 - 00:32
Mhmm.

Speaker 3 | 00:32 - 00:36
And it feels like the canonical answer Yeah. To that.

Speaker 2 | 00:36 - 00:44
Yeah. And Kevin, so it's by Kevin Roose, former New York Times, writer, currently the host of Machine Gods with Casey Newton.

Speaker 3 | 00:44 - 00:46
Which is also phenomenal.

Speaker 2 | 00:46 - 00:59
Friend of the pod. He's been on the show before. I think a great writer, and he was just basically inside of all the labs in the last decade watching them build AI, and this is his, like, canonical account of how that happened.

Speaker 3 | 00:59 - 01:37
It's not just the account of how it happened. It's also his experience as a journalist who was covering the 150 people who were tinkering to figure this out, and I just highly recommend it. You're gonna get a copy of it if you're at thesis with us on Thursday. And I think this is gonna be a book that's gonna have staying power, so I'm excited for it. Kevin, welcome to the pod.

Speaker 3 | 01:37 - 01:49
So excited to have you here. You are on such a role. I I hate to be interviewing you after you've been interviewed by Walter Isaacson and the like, but such an honor to have you here.

Speaker 1 | 01:50 - 01:52
Thanks so much for having me. This is a great honor for me too.

Speaker 3 | 01:53 - 01:59
And congratulations. Your book has been out for a few weeks and you are already a New York Times bestseller.

Speaker 1 | 02:00 - 02:19
Yeah. It's pretty wild. I have written books before that have not gone nearly this well. I think we got sort of lucky with everyone starting to care about AI, this fall when things started going haywire. So in a weird sense, I think the book has benefited from that attention.

Speaker 3 | 02:20 - 02:32
And you've spent more time than most people in the world with the, you know, 50 or so people that have really built AGI. Are we doomed? I don't think

Speaker 1 | 02:32 - 02:52
we're doomed. But we have a lot to do, if that makes sense. I think, you know, I... Part of why I wanted to write the book was to settle this question in my own mind, you know. Are we careening toward an existential cliff?

Speaker 1 | 02:52 - 03:37
Is it all hype? And the book doesn't, it's not really an attempt to settle that question, but I did learn a lot by interviewing the 50 people you mentioned plus like, you know, a 150 people in total who are sort of like connected to and involved in this scene. And I came away thinking both that there are some real risks ahead and some real needles that we'll need to thread as a society, but that we can do it. We have navigated hard challenges in our history. This is maybe one of the hardest, but I think we can do it and I don't think anything is set in stone or predestined.

Speaker 1 | 03:37 - 03:46
I think the choices that we make right now matter a lot in terms of how the next few years or few decades go.

Speaker 3 | 03:47 - 04:11
You had said a few years ago that you expected there to be some level of regulation after something went wrong. And, you know, we're there, right? A few things have gone wrong. We've had the hugging face incident and a number of other cybersecurity concerns. How do you see this going right?

Speaker 3 | 04:11 - 04:14
Right? Like, what needs to happen for us to course correct?

Speaker 1 | 04:16 - 04:46
Well, I think it's clear that we're not going to get federal regulation of AI, at least right now, from the Trump administration. I think what would need to happen for them to take a more active role is for something bad to happen. Right? We we saw this after nine eleven. We've seen this after disasters in our country's history where something that isn't on a lot of people's minds suddenly becomes the only thing people care about.

Speaker 1 | 04:46 - 05:31
We pass some, you know, congress passes some hastily written legislation or there's some executive action and we know how to do that. We know how to respond to a crisis. My hope is that we don't have to have a crisis for the government to respond, for regulatory bodies to respond. I think the first step would be to create some kind of industry standard, right? Some kind of certification program where in order to release your model or in order to deploy your model to the public, you have to kind of subject it to some standard safety testing to make sure it's not gonna go out there and do autonomous cyber attacks or be weaponized to create novel bioweapons.

Speaker 1 | 05:33 - 05:55
That seems like basic table stakes to me. We require pharmaceutical companies to test their drugs before selling them to the public. We should require AI companies to test their models before offering them to the public. So that's a first step. From there, I think you probably need some kind of a coordination mechanism for slowing down the frontier.

Speaker 1 | 05:55 - 06:34
I think this is something that I've been convinced of in the last couple of months. I didn't think it was going to be possible to slow down. I thought there were too many sort of forces pushing us toward acceleration, acceleration, acceleration. But I think we've seen from Dario and Demis and Sam and a lot of other AI leaders that they really do think this is moving too quickly. They really do want to buy the safety research teams at these companies some time to come up with new ways of controlling these systems and monitoring them so that we don't have, you know, more hugging face like incidents happening at a more regular cadence.

Speaker 3 | 06:35 - 07:17
And what I love about this book is that to some degree, for the majority of people that are engaging with AI, AI was something that kind of came out of nowhere for the majority of people. Right? You know, we're all going about our daily lives and then all of a sudden, this really kind of like hit the news in in sort of like a surprising and exciting way. And then ever since every few months, there are even more incred incredible, you know, advancements in the technology. But what was so cool about the book and about you writing this book in particular is that you've actually been tracking this story the whole time.

Speaker 3 | 07:17 - 07:35
You've been a tech reporter for over a decade And you were in the rooms as these companies were forming, as people were thinking of building these technologies. Can you tell me a little bit about what was the moment where you realized that you wanted to write this book?

Speaker 1 | 07:36 - 08:24
Well, the the moment I realized that I wanted to write this book came relatively late in the process. I was trying to avoid writing this book because I thought this is gonna be very hard. Someone's gonna have to go interview these 150 people and write down their stories, and I hope, that Walter Isaacson or someone of his stature wakes up one day and decides to write the book so that I don't have to do it. But that kept not happening, And I had a couple of motivations for eventually deciding to write the book, which I did, around the the sort of early twenty twenty five time period. One was, as you mentioned, I've been covering tech for more than a decade.

Speaker 1 | 08:24 - 09:03
I've known a lot of these AI researchers and people for a long time. I had written a previous book about AI that came out in 2021, but I really felt like I had actually not gotten the full story. I didn't know why, for example, the transformer that had been built at Google in 2017 took off at OpenAI or how that worked. I didn't know what the decision was like to release ChatGPT in 2022. I didn't know what the story behind the advent of reasoning models was in 2023.

Speaker 1 | 09:04 - 09:39
All of that seemed like historically important. Like, we we as a species should know how this stuff came into being and who was in the room and what the decisions were at the key moments. And so I thought that was useful information that I didn't have. I didn't just absorb that from tech, covering the tech industry because a lot of that was secret and a lot of it was, you know, held by people who didn't particularly want to divulge how they had done all this stuff. So I thought that was job one and then job two was to do it quickly because I thought there was some chance, some risk that all of this stuff would disappear.

Speaker 1 | 09:40 - 10:36
You know, I'm a big fan of history, I love to read books about moments in innovation, scientific breakthroughs, you know, Watson and Crick, the Wright Brothers, Marie Curie. Like, I I just... I'm obsessed with kind of the the moments where something about the fabric of the world changes or goes in a new direction because some brilliant scientist somewhere has made it so. And so my worry was that all this stuff was going to disappear because inside the labs, it's all secret, it's all under NDA, All the Slack messages and signal threads are going to delete themselves after some period of time. And I just didn't think there were gonna be a lot of records left to look back on and answer the question, how did we get here?

Speaker 1 | 10:36 - 10:45
So I thought for those reasons and because Walter Isaacson didn't wake up one day and decide to write a book about the race to AGI, I ended up doing it.

Speaker 3 | 10:46 - 11:09
Well, thank you for writing it. I certainly found it super clarifying, and I was really amazed at the level of detail that you were able to find and get to bring this story to life. How did you do that? Right? In an industry that's notoriously secretive and competitive, how did you get a 150 people to open up?

Speaker 1 | 11:10 - 11:55
Well, the first 25, I would say, were the hardest because I was really trying to appeal to some sense of historical import. These are people who get journalists reaching out to them all the time. I had talked to a number of them already for my podcast or my column, but I was really asking them to share things that they had never shared before, to tell me stories that they had never told before. And so part of how I made them comfortable enough to to do that was by giving them the ability to speak to me on background. So, that was how I conducted the majority of interviews for this book.

Speaker 1 | 11:55 - 12:41
I would say, you know, I'm not gonna name you as a source. I'm not going to identify you as the person who's giving me this information. I'm just going to kind of use it to construct this narrative. And they were very, you know, a lot of them were willing to do that, some of them were still unwilling to do that, and so I had to kind of give them other guarantees or, you know, other reassurances that I wasn't going to turn around and write some book about how, you know, they were all horrible people or something. But then something interesting happened after the first, I don't know, '25 or 50 where it started to snowball because these people all talk, it's a very small world, and they would say, oh, are you are you talking to Kevin Roose, for his book?

Speaker 1 | 12:42 - 13:11
Oh, yeah, I I talked to him. Oh, well then maybe I should talk to him too. Or, you know, some some people would actually be motivated to talk to me because someone that they hate had talked to me. So it was like, if that guy's talking to you, giving you his side of the story, I wanna make sure that I give you my side of the story too. But then I think the bigger tactic was just being really sincere and doing the reading.

Speaker 1 | 13:11 - 13:50
Like, reading the researchers papers before I went to talk to them so that I could ask them the right questions and get at the level of detail that you kindly noted that I got to where I was like, I I I wanted to know very specific things about this story as it has unfolded at these three AI companies. And, you know, I I think it it matters when a journalist shows up and they're like, you know, citing other interviews they've done or papers they've written and it just demonstrates to them that I was serious about this, that I just I didn't just want kind of the surface level overview. I wanted to, like, go deep on a few things.

Speaker 2 | 13:51 - 14:09
If you like this video, you should check out Every. T o. We have a two week free trial for anyone who's watching or listening at the link in the description. Every is the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI. It is the one subscription that if you're super AI pill and you wanna learn how to use it to do the best work of your life, it's got everything you need.

Speaker 2 | 14:09 - 14:27
It has education and equipment. On the education side, we review every new model that drops and tell you what's good. On the equipment side, we have software tools specifically made for you, like an agent that helps you AI pillar your whole company, all bundled together under one subscription. So get two weeks free now at the link in the description.

Speaker 3 | 14:27 - 15:17
I'd love to do a really quick aside on the sources because it's so clear to me reading this book that the amount of reading that you must have done to like really wrap your head around the types of technology that got developed in order for AI to get to what it is today and the types of inventions, you know, were, they're really complex, right? And they weren't obvious that we would have discovered them in the way that we did. What were... What are like your one to three favorite papers or books or resources that you found that you found most delightful or informative, or you kind of recommend... Would recommend to other people to like go back and read beyond your book?

Speaker 1 | 15:19 - 15:40
Yeah. I mean, some of them were things that had never been published before that I found through reporting, such as this... I I I'm... I I love this memo called the big blob of compute hypothesis. This was something that Dario Amade wrote when he was at OpenAI before starting Anthropic in 2017.

Speaker 1 | 15:41 - 16:10
So this is very early in the AI race. Large language models hadn't even been invented yet. But Dario, who was then the vice president of research at OpenAI, wrote this sort of internally famous memo. Like everyone at OpenAI remembers reading this memo because it really it really reshaped their roadmap and their ambitions. At the time, lot of AI research was going into these sort of narrow approaches.

Speaker 1 | 16:10 - 16:44
Right? If you wanted to build a system that, you know, would beat the best human Go players like DeepMind did the year before. You would like build a customized system, know, make some sort of architectural improvements to that system and then like train your model to do that one thing very very well. Dario sort of looked out at the landscape and I think in a way that was incredibly prescient, said, I think you're all doing this wrong. I don't think we should be training these narrow models.

Speaker 1 | 16:45 - 17:28
I think we should be assembling these large unstructured masses of computational capacity, as he put it, otherwise known as big blobs of compute. And we should be pointing them at general problems, like predict the next word in a sentence, or, you know, or other sort of much more general problems and trusting that sort of intelligence would result from that process. So I love this memo. I published like the first 10 pages of it on on my substack, people can find it. But I think it is like a true artifact where like you see in almost real time, like the light bulb going off in Dario's head where he's like, oh, we should just scale these models.

Speaker 1 | 17:28 - 18:01
And if we do nothing else, we will be able to figure out whether it's true that bigger models create more intelligent behavior. Other ones I really liked, there's this book, by Arthur C. Clarke, that was sort of, you know, a precursor to a lot of what happened at OpenAI. I actually can't remember the name now, but I went back and read it. It was something about the future and it was a book that Ilya Satskever, the former chief scientist of OpenAI, really loved.

Speaker 1 | 18:01 - 18:33
So I went back and read that and basically you understand, you know, when you read this why people at OpenAI loved it, because the whole point of at least the introduction to the book is like talking about how that, you know, every time there's some new breakthrough technology, there are these sort of wizened old men who say like, oh, that's impossible, that's never going to happen and then it happens and it's sort of the vindication of the crazy science fiction true believers. So they felt connected to that book. I... Yeah. I went back.

Speaker 1 | 18:33 - 19:28
I read a lot of science fiction. I read The Making of the Atomic Bomb was a book that was weirdly central in the AI race because it's this incredible, Pulitzer winning history by Richard Rhodes of the Manhattan Project. And again, Dario read this book as a a young man and it really shaped him. He really identified with this character Leo Szilard who was Hungarian American scientist, physicist who basically discovers the nuclear chain reaction, fights to keep it secret, and then when it gets out to the Nazis, he joins the Manhattan Project and tries to build the bomb before the Nazis do. And this is a, like, a central story in Dario's life because he sees himself as a modern day Leo Szalar.

Speaker 1 | 19:28 - 19:39
He is working to build this technology in part to keep it out of the hands of the bad guys or to keep them from building it first. So those are some of the books that that I liked.

Speaker 3 | 19:39 - 19:42
I'm excited to dig into those. Thanks for sharing.

Speaker 1 | 19:42 - 19:46
Profiles of the future. That's the Arthur C. Clarke book. Sorry.

Speaker 3 | 19:46 - 20:07
I was curious just kind of looking into your background that... I believe your mom is also an author. She wrote a book about kind of like retelling the stories or or rather just telling the stories of the survivors of the first atomic bomb. Is that correct?

Speaker 1 | 20:08 - 20:28
Yeah. She wrote a book. She she did a lot of research on the habakasha, which is the Japanese term for the survivors of the the, you know, the atomic bomb in Japan. And so, yeah, she talked to a bunch of survivors about their experiences and collected them into a into a really great book.

Speaker 3 | 20:31 - 20:47
Because you call AGI kind of like our era's Manhattan Project, I was curious if you ever found any parallels between your mom's work and you kind of telling the story of our Manhattan Project and how we are digesting and managing AGI.

Speaker 1 | 20:48 - 21:52
It's a really good question and it is the rare question that I've never been asked before, so I'm really glad you raised it. I did not consciously model this book on my mom's work on the Habakkasha. But I think it was obviously formative for me to grow up in a house where there was someone doing sort of real time history and record keeping. And I think part of what motivated her was the sense that these people weren't gonna live forever, and it was very important to hear from the firsthand witnesses to something as important as the atomic bomb because that brought the story to life in a new way. So I think on some subconscious level, I probably was, you know, doing something similar, and I wasn't worried that the AI researchers were going to die and that their stories would die with them, but it was sort of motivated by the same sense of like, somebody's gotta write this down because it's really important that people understand, what happened.

Speaker 1 | 21:52 - 22:01
Either, you know, in in her case, I think it was so that we could avoid doing that again. In my case, it was just like, I think that we deserve to know how this technology was built.

Speaker 3 | 22:03 - 22:16
One of the terms that you use in the book is, you know, I I believe it's Ilya uses the phrase like when did you feel the AGI or do you feel the AGI? When did you first feel AGI?

Speaker 1 | 22:18 - 22:19
Feel the AGI.

Speaker 3 | 22:19 - 22:20
The AGI.

Speaker 1 | 22:21 - 22:53
You must feel... He he would he would... Ilya would walk desk to desk at OpenAI and just go, you must feel the AGI, you know, and people sort of came to treat him and see him as sort of like a high priest. You know, he would just walk around with his mantras. I think I started to feel it in 2023 when I had this encounter with Bing Sydney, which was the deranged alter ego of Microsoft's Bing chat function.

Speaker 1 | 22:53 - 23:10
And, you know, that was a noteworthy event in my life. It got a lot of attention. It, you know, became, you know, the most popular thing I ever wrote or will ever write. But I think it was also the time where I realized, like, oh, this is... This feels different.

Speaker 1 | 23:10 - 23:51
This does not feel like, an inert tool. I didn't think it was sentient or conscious or alive, but I thought, well, this is a powerful technology on a social level as well as a technological and economic level. And I just felt like that was when I needed to understand more about not only how these systems are built and what they're doing under the hood, but the companies and the people that are racing to put them out into the world. In some cases, cutting corners because they're so eager to beat their rivals and why? Why why are they so eager to beat their...

Speaker 1 | 23:51 - 23:56
You know, what are they all racing toward? I think that was sort of the the time when I started asking that question.

Speaker 3 | 23:57 - 24:19
The last time you were on the pod, Kevin, you were telling us about some of the ways in which you are using AI. And, you know, of of... One of the things about this book that's actually most impressive to me is that you wrote 450 pages in a year. That's a lot of writing. But, we asked you about how...

Speaker 3 | 24:19 - 24:30
About your writing process and, how it's evolved. And I'd love for you to tell us a little bit about how you're using AI today and also how it's evolved since you first started using it.

Speaker 1 | 24:32 - 25:02
Yeah. Well, I'll start by just saying a thing that I hope is obvious. It might not be obvious, but, which is a way that I didn't use AI was to write the book. So all the words are from this brain and these fingers and I I did not feel like it was a book that I wanted to give over to AI to to do the actual writing. I did use AI for basically everything else.

Speaker 1 | 25:02 - 25:48
I mean, had human editors, a human researcher, Jasmine Sun, who's wonderful. I had a lot of, like, skilled expertise involved in making this, But it was hard and it took a long time and as you mentioned, it's a very long book and I earned every, you know, every wrinkle on my forehead writing it in a year. But I guess a few ways that I used it that might be novel or surprising. One was I had a council of Claude's that would review chapters when I finished the draft. I would feed it into Cloud Code which I had set up to run this sort of swarm of agents.

Speaker 1 | 25:49 - 26:20
I assigned each of these agents a persona or a perspective. So, you know, one might be an AI skeptic who just doesn't think LLMs are actually intelligent. One might be, you know, an AI historian who's like a really expert at all of the sort of technical precursors to all the systems I'm writing about and can correct me if I get something wrong. One was sort of a Walter Isaacson style, like crafts person who just is interested in like, how does this flow? What is the storytelling arc?

Speaker 1 | 26:21 - 26:51
Is it a is it a joy to read? And so I would have a master editor agent kind of synthesize the... What the Council of Claude said and present me with sort of a, you know, a a written through synthetic document about what it thought of the chapter I'd just, you know, turned into the council. And that was fairly useful at times. It did catch a couple of factual errors, that I had not caught and my human editors had not caught and, and that was surprising.

Speaker 1 | 26:51 - 27:17
I think that shows the evolution of the tools because a couple years ago, you know, we had to fact check the AIs and now the AIs fact check me. And that just shows how much more capable the systems have become. The hallucination rates have gone way down. They're much better at grounding what they are telling you in real sources, pulled from real documents. So that was one area.

Speaker 1 | 27:17 - 28:03
And then just in terms of organizing a sprawling research project, like, I could not have written this book without tools like NotebookLM, which allowed me to just sort of dump all of my research material into a notebook or a series of notebooks and just ask questions, help me spot connections. Know, I could say, you know, who told me that story about the pre training of GPT-four? Or who are the three people I should contact to learn more about this thing that happened at Anthropic in 2021? And it would comb through every, you know, piece of source material I had and give me a recommendation. So that was incredibly helpful.

Speaker 1 | 28:04 - 28:31
You know, I I use this stuff every day. I've got, like, three or four agents running right now doing various tasks for me. And, you know, everything from, like, little projects for the the startup I'm building with with Casey Newton and also things about just my daily life and doing admin tasks and arranging, you know, childcare and things like that. So it's it's doing a lot for me.

Speaker 3 | 28:32 - 28:50
To what extent do you feel like your role as a writer has evolved and kind of become amplified? Right? Because you were at the New York Times for a decade. You had access to some of the best editors in the world. But at some point, you also started codifying what a good editor does and looks for.

Speaker 3 | 28:50 - 29:03
Right? In in giving instructions to the agents that you've set up to do this work for you. And it sounds like you have a number of agents. So at some point, you have to do the thinking of what are the roles that matter? What does it mean to do this role well?

Speaker 3 | 29:03 - 29:10
How has that evolved? How you think about your role as writer and how it's amplified? What else you think about in your creative process?

Speaker 1 | 29:13 - 29:39
Yeah. I I think an editor can do a lot of things. Right? And and the best human editors do a lot of things. They are skilled at line editing, at spotting places where things could be sharpened or tightened or expanded on, at thinking about structure and pacing and where, you know, how to deliver information in a way that is gonna be satisfying for the reader.

Speaker 1 | 29:40 - 29:53
But they're also coaches. They also motivate you. They tell you it doesn't feel like you've really cracked this yet. Go back to your sources and try to figure this out yet. So that is part of the editor's job.

Speaker 1 | 29:53 - 30:17
Also just having kind of the ability to say this story is worth pursuing, this story maybe is less worth pursuing. So I think of the best editors I've worked with in my career, all of whom are human, as sort of compilations of those skills. And AI can't do a lot of that yet. It can do the line editing great. It's really really good at line editing.

Speaker 1 | 30:17 - 30:40
It's it's it's getting better at things like pacing and structure, but, you know, you you need both. At least I need both to produce something that I'm really proud of. I need the the line editing, the sort of technical editing work, and then I also need the coaching, the inspiration, the motivation, the like, hey, go back. It doesn't feel like you've totally gotten that one yet.

Speaker 3 | 30:42 - 30:53
Tell me a little bit more about the tools that you're using. Are you still primarily in Claude Code? Are you in Codex? Are you using some of the more packaged personal agents? Like, what specifically are you playing with today?

Speaker 1 | 30:54 - 31:07
I'm playing with everything. Literally, like, I can't keep track. I have agents now that are, like, correcting my other agents. It's a huge mess. I need to do some calling.

Speaker 1 | 31:07 - 31:33
But, yeah, I'm using, right now Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini for some things. I'm using ChatGPT dot. I'm using Town, which is a sort of enterprise agent that Casey got me hooked on. I've got... I'm doing various vibe coding projects just as a side thing on the weekends.

Speaker 1 | 31:34 - 31:56
I'm running I'm running local models to do things like transcription and summarization. Obviously, everyone's got, you know, the the granola note taking stack that feeds into your, you know, personal CRM. So I'm I'm like... You know, it's my job to test stuff, and I also really like testing stuff. And so I'm I'm using kind of everything you can imagine.

Speaker 3 | 31:57 - 32:01
And today, when you sit down to write, what app are you using?

Speaker 1 | 32:03 - 32:06
I am mostly using Google Docs.

Speaker 3 | 32:07 - 32:08
Okay.

Speaker 1 | 32:08 - 32:37
You know, it is... It has many issues. But for just pure, like, I wanna quickly open up a doc, and these days I'm I'm usually writing for the show, so I'm writing with producers in the doc too. So it just is the best way. I did experiment with using sort of more specialized writing apps like Scrivener and stuff in the past, but for me, it has always been Google Docs.

Speaker 3 | 32:39 - 32:49
So you didn't just publish this New York Times bestselling book. You also just launched a new podcast. Can you tell us a little bit about that?

Speaker 1 | 32:50 - 33:05
Yeah. So the new new show is called Machine Gods. We are publishing two episodes a week. We just started last week, but we're already, you know, very happy with how the show's doing. We're making it in partnership with NPR, which is really fun.

Speaker 1 | 33:05 - 33:42
And it's me and Casey Newton, my longtime cohost on Hard Fork. We are now treating AI as the most important story in the world, which it is. So our, you know, our our our episode last week, we interviewed the the two of the three safety researchers formerly at OpenAI who were fired after some dispute about, you know, information sharing with external auditors. We plan to continue to analyze the news of the week, to interview newsmakers in AI, and just try to make things fun and accessible for people.

Speaker 3 | 33:44 - 33:56
It's so cool that you have this platform now, but how do you keep up with technology but also maintain this sense of creativity and wonder as, you know, all of these tools evolve?

Speaker 1 | 33:57 - 34:25
You just have to like the tools, I think. I mean, I I grew up, I was a big computer kid. I had, you know, I I built web pages with my brother when I was like 10 or 11 years old.
